tldr: "Reward hacking," where robots exploit shortcuts during reinforcement learning, does not just happen in rewards. It occurs across four distinct layers: curriculum gates, evaluation statistics, and reference motions. This paper mathematically clarifies the divergence mechanism at each layer and offers practical recipes to train a humanoid policy from scratch without failure on a single GPU.
overview:
With the rise of GPU-accelerated simulators, training a walking policy for a humanoid robot takes only a few hours. Yet researchers building these learning pipelines often run into bizarre behaviors: a policy that slowly drifts forward while stepping in place, a curriculum gate that rushes to maximum difficulty while the target skill is entirely absent, or a robot showing higher fall rates under gentle pushes than violent ones.

Traditionally, these issues have been dismissed as minor reward tuning failures (reward hacking) or random-seed variance. The author points out that all of them stem from the same root: divergence introduced by replacing true physical objectives with convenient, computable proxies. Optimization pressure acts not just on rewards; curriculum promotion gates, evaluation scripts, and imitation reference motions are all proxies. Each produces its own characteristic bugs (divergences).

Through experiments spanning 13,500 iterations training a 1.91 m tall humanoid in simulation, the author mathematically derives the divergence conditions at each layer and presents field-ready reformulations. Paired with an "input widening" method that avoids retraining when the observation space expands, the paper demonstrates a complete, uninterrupted multi-stage training run on a single laptop GPU (RTX 5070 Ti).
contributions: Formulated reinforcement learning pipeline failures systematically as proxy divergences across four layers: reward, curriculum, measurement, and reference motions, providing formal divergence conditions and corrections for each.

Proved the "dilution bound" where averaged errors in curriculum gates mask catastrophic single-joint failures, and established pre-checks for gate information content (refusal rate) and reference motion reachability.

Identified and resolved measurement biases that do not vanish with larger sample sizes, such as phase aliasing caused by synchronized resets in parallel simulators and false successes manufactured by exploration noise.
Demonstrated why reward shaping cannot fix dynamically infeasible reference motions, proposing feasibility-first correction and residual feed-forward control as the solution.
Proposed and validated "input widening," a method that lets a policy absorb new observation dimensions without retraining from scratch.

sections.heading: Traps Hiding in the Reinforcement Learning Plumbing
sections.summary: In robot reinforcement learning, rewards, curriculum promotion gates, robustness metrics, and reference motions all serve as proxies for physical goals. This paper systematically explores how these four proxy layers diverge from intended behavior and how to fix them.
sections.details:
GPU-accelerated parallel simulation allows controllers for bipedal robots to be trained in a few hours on a single machine. Today's standard pipeline typically combines multi-term weighted rewards, curricula conditioned on terrain or velocity commands, batch evaluations in simulation, and reference motion tracking terms. Each of these components replaces an intended physical phenomenon with a convenient numerical proxy.

The reinforcement learning community has traditionally treated specification gaming exclusively as a reward function issue—namely, reward hacking. Curriculum gates are treated as mere hyperparameters, evaluation scripts as faithful instruments, and reference motions as achievable targets.

The author argues that this view is fundamentally incomplete. Policies survive only if they pass curriculum gates, which means the gate itself experiences implicit optimization pressure just like a reward. Evaluation scripts can introduce systematic biases purely through poor test-harness design, completely independent of optimization. Furthermore, if a reference motion is dynamically impossible, no amount of reward tuning will guide the robot to the target skill.

### Core Contributions
This paper mathematically shows why traditional formulations fail across all four layers (reward, curriculum, measurement, and reference) and introduces concrete, practical alternatives. It also proposes an "input widening" technique to continuously grow a policy when the observation space expands, validating the entire pipeline on a single laptop GPU.

sections.heading: Lineage of Robot Learning, Specification Gaming, and Network Growth
sections.summary: This section surveys existing work in deep RL for legged robots and specification gaming, framing the paper as an extension of these concepts beyond the reward layer into network growth and evaluation design.
sections.details:
Deep reinforcement learning (Deep RL) has delivered impressive milestones in legged locomotion and humanoid control, from zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to agile whole-body behaviors. Most research pipelines rely on GPU-parallel simulation platforms such as Isaac Lab.

In reward design and specification gaming, researchers have long documented the difficulty of crafting unhackable proxy rewards, as well as the tendency of capable agents to over-optimize misspecified objectives. However, prior work focused almost exclusively on the reward function, overlooking the fact that curriculum gates, evaluation statistics, and reference trajectories are also proxies subject to divergence.

Regarding evaluation, past literature focused on variance—such as random-seed sensitivity and statistical spread. This paper targets systematic bias, which does not diminish no matter how many rollout samples are gathered.

For continuous learning across changing observation spaces, the paper builds on ideas like Net2Net and Plasticity Injection to preserve existing function while extending the input dimension directly.

sections.heading: The Experimental Setup: A 1.91 m Humanoid
sections.summary: Using a 1.91 m tall, ~69 kg humanoid model imported directly from CAD, the policy is trained using PPO across 2048 parallel environments. The entire multi-stage training pipeline runs on a single laptop GPU (RTX 5070 Ti Laptop).
sections.details:
The experimental platform is a full-scale humanoid model derived directly from CAD assemblies, measuring 1.91 m in height and weighing 69.35 kg. The policy controls 11 degrees of freedom (DoF) focused on the lower body: hip pitch/roll, knee, ankle pitch/roll for both legs, and waist yaw. The remaining 10 DoFs (arms and neck) are outside the policy's authority and driven by independent position commands.

The policy network is a 3-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) with 128 ELU units per layer, trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE; discount factor $\gamma=0.99$, $\lambda=0.95$). Physics runs at 200 Hz while the policy operates at 50 Hz, gathering rollouts across 2048 environments with 24 steps per iteration.

Observations include base linear and angular velocities, projected gravity vectors, velocity commands, joint states, previous actions, and a 187-ray terrain height scan. Notably, all multi-stage training stages were conducted on a single laptop GPU (RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU).

The paper defines a proxy $m$ as a computable quantity substituted for a physical target $T$ to guide or measure training, and formalizes proxy divergence as the condition where $m$ indicates success while $T$ remains unfulfilled.

sections.heading: Reward Layer Divergence: Flat Kernels and Unbounded Joints
sections.summary: Smooth Gaussian kernels have zero gradient near zero-velocity targets, allowing steady forward drift. Unconstrained joints will pin themselves against hard limits unless penalized or given explicit command targets.
sections.details:
### IV-A First-Order Drift Under Quadratic Kernels
To build smooth, bounded rewards for velocity tracking, researchers frequently use Gaussian kernels: $r_{\mathrm{trk}}=\exp(-\|\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{v}\|^{2}/\sigma^{2})$, where $\mathbf{c}$ is the commanded velocity and $\mathbf{v}$ is actual base velocity. When the command is to stand still ($\mathbf{c}=0$), this formulation produces a major flaw.

For a bipedal humanoid, maintaining balance by continuously stepping or creeping forward at a small drift velocity $v$ is often easier than remaining perfectly static. Let $g(v)$ denote the auxiliary rewards gained by moving; its derivative at the origin is often positive ($g'(0) > 0$). Meanwhile, the Gaussian kernel has a quadratic flat bottom with a derivative of zero at $v=0$. Consequently, total reward is maximized at a non-zero velocity rather than at rest. With a bandwidth of $\sigma=0.5$, drifting forward at 0.2 m/s still earns a tracking reward of 0.85, causing the robot to creep forward persistently despite a zero-velocity command.

The fix is straightforward: couple zero-velocity tracking with a first-order (L1 norm, $-\lambda |v|$) penalty that has a sharp, non-zero gradient at the origin. Adding an L1 base velocity penalty with weight 1.5 cut the measured drift down to 0.01–0.04 m/s.

### IV-B Unconstrained Coordinates Pin to Hard Limits
To curb unwanted movements, engineers often penalize specific joints while ignoring others. If a joint $q_j$ is omitted entirely from the reward terms, the policy uses it however physics makes easiest. If coupling from other reward terms exerts monotonic pressure on that joint, it will drift until it slams into its mechanical range limit.

During rough-terrain training, omitting waist yaw penalties caused the yaw joint to pin against its $+45.00^{\circ}$ limit on 100% of steps with zero variance. Crucially, overall return and fall rates appeared to improve (fall rates dropped from 5.3% to 2.8%), masking the failure.

The remedy is to ensure every actuated joint is covered by the reward's support. In the final setup, waist yaw was placed under active tracking commands ($\pm 0.7$ rad, commanding zero half the time) rather than passive penalization.

sections.heading: Curriculum Layer Divergence: Catastrophic Errors Diluted by Averages
sections.summary: Curriculum gates based on errors averaged across all joints and time steps can easily pass policies with critical joint failures. Gates should use peak errors combined with physical contact checks, while tracking refusal counts.
sections.details:
### V-A The Dilution Bound on Averaged Error
Curricula commonly promote difficulty whenever the recent mean tracking error $\bar{e}$ drops below a threshold $\tau$. Averaging error across all joints $|\mathcal{J}|$ and time steps $T$, however, creates a critical blind spot.

Suppose a single key joint deviates by $e^{\ast}$ over a fraction $\rho$ of the episode, while all other joints track nearly perfectly (error $\le \epsilon$). The overall mean error is bounded by $\rho e^{\ast}/|\mathcal{J}| + \epsilon$. Thus, the threshold condition $\bar{e} < \tau$ will pass any failure satisfying $e^{\ast} < |\mathcal{J}|(\tau - \epsilon)/\rho$. With 10 joints, $\tau=0.25$ rad, and $\rho\approx 0.3$, a joint can deviate by several radians without tripping the gate. In one-legged balance experiments, the hip error on the lifted leg reached 59 degrees ($\approx 1.03$ rad), yet the gate recorded a mean error of only 0.06–0.07 rad and advanced at maximum speed. Because both feet stayed on the ground, fall detection never triggered.

The solution is to evaluate gates using peak error ($e_\infty$) restricted to the active joint subset, paired with outcome-based predicates such as requiring foot contact force to stay below 1 N.

### V-B Information Content and Promotion Refusal
If a curriculum gate never rejects a policy, its information-theoretic entropy is zero ($H(G)=0$), providing no evidence of the robot's true competence ($C$). Training logs revealed that 7 curriculum stages promoted at exactly their rate limit (every ~41.7 iterations) with zero refusals. This meant the curriculum effectively did nothing. Refusals must be actively logged; a gate that never refuses promotion is untrustworthy.

### V-C Pre-checking Gate Reachability
Is a target threshold $\tau$ physically reachable by any policy? Playing the reference motion open-loop ($\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$) in simulation tests reachability in a single rollout. In this work, the test revealed that initial foot-lift targets were too low: slight compliance in the stance leg caused the foot to drag, making a 50% flight-phase requirement physically impossible under the original parameters.

### V-D Curriculum State Belongs to the Model
Saving only network weights and optimizer states treats curriculum difficulty as ephemeral environment state. If a checkpoint fine-tunes from level zero, previously mastered high-difficulty behaviors lose their training signals. The curriculum stage $k$ must be serialized as part of the model state.

sections.heading: Measurement Layer Divergence: Noise Illusions and Aliased Resets
sections.summary: Exploration noise can manufacture artificial metric successes, and synchronized parallel resets alias the gait phase, severely distorting disturbance evaluations. Both issues are proven analytically and verified experimentally.
sections.details:
### VI-A False Success Manufactured by Exploration Noise
During training, actions include stochastic exploration noise: $a = \mu_\theta(s) + \sigma \varepsilon$. If leg clearance milestones are tracked during training rollouts, high noise on the ankles (fluctuations around $\pm 40^{\circ}$) can pop the robot onto its toes, raising the center of mass above the threshold even though the deterministic policy $\mu_\theta$ never lifts the foot. Training logs reported reaching 61–69% of target clearance, but deterministic rollouts revealed zero clearance. Evaluations must use deterministic policies and verify true physical flight via contact force thresholds (< 1 N).

### VI-B Phase Aliasing in Batched Evaluations
Robustness tests in parallel simulators typically reset all $N$ environments simultaneously, settle for $t_0$, and apply a lateral push. Because walking is periodic with period $P$, synchronized resets mean every robot receives the disturbance at the exact same point in its gait cycle (e.g., exclusively during left-foot stance).

This systematic bias does not decrease by scaling $N$ to thousands of robots; it simply measures an unrepresentative number with higher precision. In tests, a 0.5 m/s push yielded an 88% fall rate, while a 2.0 m/s push yielded only 50%, alongside extreme left-right asymmetry. Uniformly randomizing disturbance timings across a window wider than the gait cycle ($W=1$ s) eliminated this phase lock, restoring expected monotonicity and left-right symmetry.

### VI-C Quantifier Mismatches in Aggregate Statistics
Claiming omnidirectional push recovery requires reporting the worst-case fall rate across all directions (a universal quantifier, $\forall$). If evaluation scripts instead report the highest disturbance survived in any single direction (an existential quantifier, $\exists$), severe vulnerabilities—such as a 38% fall rate in one direction—are masked behind false robustness claims.

sections.heading: Reference Motion Layer Divergence: Unfeasible Trajectories Cannot Be Tracked
sections.summary: Reward shaping cannot force a policy to follow a statically impossible reference motion; the policy will simply diverge toward alternative behaviors. Trajectories must be verified and corrected kinematically, then provided as residual feed-forward terms.
sections.details:
### Optimization Against Impossible Trajectories Causes Qualitative Collapse
When teaching complex skills, researchers often provide a hand-crafted reference trajectory $q_{\mathrm{ref}}(t)$ and reward tracking. But if this trajectory lies outside the physically realizable set $\mathcal{F}$, failure is guaranteed.

To avoid termination penalties, the policy projects the impossible reference onto the nearest feasible motion in $\mathcal{F}$ under its reward metric. There is no guarantee that this projection preserves the qualitative features of the reference, such as contact schedules or single-leg balance. A hand-crafted one-legged stance reference respected joint limits but placed the horizontal Center of Mass (CoM) 0.21 m outside the support foot. Across 7 parameter variants, not a single deterministic policy achieved one-legged balance.

### Recipe 1: Feasibility First
Before adjusting rewards, verify static equilibrium across keyframes (i.e., whether the horizontal CoM projection lies inside the support polygon). Measuring stance-leg roll showed that tilting moved the CoM by ~0.0095 m per degree, indicating a necessary roll of $\theta \approx 0.21 / 0.0095 \approx 22^{\circ}$. Introducing a kinematically feasible $20^{\circ}$ stance roll reduced CoM offset to just 0.02 m. Verifying this corrected motion in open-loop simulation ensured correct contact schedules before RL began.

### Recipe 2: Residual Feed-Forward
Once a feasible reference is available, feeding it directly into joint targets relieves the policy from discovering the trajectory from scratch:
$q^{\ast}(t) = q_0 + r(t) + 0.5 a$
(where $r(t)$ is reference offset and $a$ is policy action). When $a=0$, the robot tracks the target motion directly, shifting the policy's role from broad exploration to balance regulation. Policies trained without feed-forward only leaned the stance leg by $-1^{\circ}$ to $-3^{\circ}$, whereas policies with residual feed-forward maintained stable single-leg flight from the start.

sections.heading: Growing the Policy: Input Widening and Authority Partitioning
sections.summary: Zero-padding weights allows expanding observation dimensions without performance regression or retraining. Combining this with observation of unactuated upper-body joints enables uninterrupted multi-stage skill acquisition.
sections.details:
### VIII-A Function-Preserving Input Widening
As development progresses, adding new sensory inputs or reference offsets to the observation space is often necessary. Changing input dimensions normally invalidates existing checkpoints, forcing engineers to restart training.

The author addresses this by concatenating new inputs $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}$ to the end of the observation vector and zero-padding the corresponding weights in the first layers of both actor and critic. This ensures identical policy outputs and value predictions at the moment of expansion, preserving prior skills completely. Unlike zero-initialized hidden layers, padded first-layer weights receive gradients immediately from the first update step ($\partial L / \partial W_{\mathrm{new}} = \boldsymbol{\delta} \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{new}}^{\top}$). Expanding inputs from 253 to 274 dimensions preserved existing outputs within a tolerance of $10^{-5}$.

### VIII-B Authority Partitioning and External Motion Observation
If an unactuated upper body is kept completely frozen during locomotion training, moving the arms on hardware introduces severe distribution shifts. In experiments, humanoids trained with frozen arms tipped over immediately when their arms were extended outward due to unexpected lateral moments.

By driving upper-body joints with random kinematic sequences during training and including their positions and velocities in the lower-body policy's observations, the policy learns to treat upper-body motions as predictable disturbances, counteracting their inertia with the legs.

### VIII-C The Validated Policy Lineage
Using these methods, four distinct stages—S1 (quiet standing and upper-body compensation), S2 (velocity tracking curriculum up to 2 m/s), S3 (fast upper-body motion tracking), and S4 (residual tracking with 21-dim reference motion via input widening)—were trained in a single uninterrupted policy lineage without resets. The entire four-stage pipeline finished in 14.2 hours using $6.6 \times 10^8$ samples on a single laptop GPU.

sections.heading: Pipeline Checkup: Traditional Formulations Versus Proposed Solutions
sections.summary: This section tabulates the divergence mechanisms across all four layers alongside their proposed reformulations, serving as a practical audit checklist for reinforcement learning pipeline design.
sections.details:
The key items in the four-layer proxy audit checklist are:

- **Reward Layer**:
  - Traditional Gaussian kernels for static targets cause drift due to zero gradients; pair with first-order (L1) costs at the origin.
  - Unpenalized coordinates pin to mechanical limits; include every controlled DoF in the reward support or provide active commands.

- **Curriculum Layer**:
  - Averaged error across all joints and time steps dilutes local failures; gate on peak error ($L_\infty$) restricted to target joints and require physical contact predicates.
  - Zero-refusal gates carry no information; explicitly log refusal counts.
  - Unrealistic thresholds lead to dead ends; compute reachability beforehand using open-loop reference playback.
  - Environment-managed curriculum progress shifts objectives during fine-tuning; store curriculum level inside checkpoints.

- **Measurement Layer**:
  - Testing during noisy training rollouts creates false positives; evaluate using deterministic policies and physical predicates.
  - Synchronous parallel resets alias the gait phase; desynchronize disturbance application over a full gait cycle.
  - Existential metrics mask vulnerabilities; evaluate using worst-case (universal) bounds across all directions.

- **Reference Motion Layer**:
  - Tracking dynamically impossible motions causes policy collapse; pre-correct static/dynamic feasibility and inject references via residual feed-forward.

sections.heading: Why Has Reinforcement Learning Fixated on Rewards Alone?
sections.summary: The RL community has focused on reward hacking under the assumption that only rewards receive optimization pressure. The other three layers must receive equal verification scrutiny.
sections.details:
Why has research focused almost exclusively on reward design while overlooking bugs in curriculum gates, evaluation scripts, and reference trajectories? The standard intuition was that because optimization algorithms only backpropagate gradients from the reward, specification gaming could only happen there.

As this paper shows, however, policies that survive flawed curriculum gates or exploit exploration noise to pass benchmarks are also experiencing implicit optimization pressure. Furthermore, measurement flaws like phase aliasing and existential aggregation produce massive systematic errors regardless of optimization.

In all these cases, flawed pipeline plumbing reports apparent success when real tasks remain unsolved. Engineers must scrutinize their measurement harnesses and curriculum gates with the same skepticism traditionally reserved for reward functions.

Crucially, most proposed fixes require negligible compute overhead: open-loop sanity checks, small random delays in test scripts, and minimal checkpoint adjustments are all lightweight to implement.

sections.heading: Summary: Building Policies on Honest Numbers
sections.summary: Failures in legged robot learning span all four pipeline layers, not just rewards. Principled reformulations and input widening allow robust humanoid policies to be trained on a modest laptop GPU.
sections.details:
The assumption that specification failure in legged locomotion is confined to reward functions is incorrect. Curriculum gates, evaluation scripts, and reference motions are all proxies for physical competence, each susceptible to distinct failure modes.

- First-order (L1) penalties at zero-velocity targets
- Reachable curriculum gates evaluated via peak errors and physical contact predicates
- Curriculum states tracked directly within model checkpoints
- Deterministic, phase-desynchronized evaluation harnesses
- Kinematically verified reference motions integrated via residual feed-forward
- Progressive policy growth via function-preserving input widening

Adopting these practices keeps every numerical signal in the training loop grounded, helping roboticists escape trial-and-error rabbit holes. Successfully training a full-scale humanoid across multiple stages on a single laptop GPU proves that robust RL pipelines depend on sound formulation rather than massive compute clusters.

takeaways: Always pair zero-velocity Gaussian tracking rewards with an L1 cost; the flat quadratic bottom allows persistent first-order creeping drift.

Never use tracking errors averaged over all joints and time steps to advance curriculum gates. Averaging dilutes severe single-joint failures; rely on peak errors (L-infinity) and contact predicates instead.
Desynchronize push-disturbance timings across at least one full gait cycle during batch evaluations to prevent phase aliasing from synchronized environment resets.
Reward shaping cannot salvage dynamically infeasible reference motions. Kinematically correct the motion beforehand and apply it as a residual feed-forward target.
Expand observation dimensions by zero-padding the first layer's weights (input widening) to retain full checkpoint performance without restarting training.
limitations: All experiments were conducted purely within physics simulation using a single random seed; direct sim-to-real transfer onto a physical humanoid robot was not evaluated.

Robot inertial properties were calculated assuming uniform solid density from CAD models, and actuator dynamics did not include real-world motor characteristics such as torque limits and joint backlash.
